subtitulo: Occupation, famine, resistance, and the extermination of the Jewish community of Corfu (1941–1944)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for

items.text: In Corfu, go to the Evraikí quarter, behind the New Fortress. The Scuola Greca synagogue is open to visitors at limited hours, and the present-day community numbers only a few dozen people. In Solomou Square there is a monument to the victims, with an inscription recalling June 9, 1944. It is an unassuming site, without prominent tourist signage, and precisely for that reason it is worth seeking out. As you walk through the Old Fortress as a sightseeing attraction, keep in mind that it was the assembly point before the deportation.

In Athens, if it interests you, the Jewish Museum of Greece in Plaka is small and excellent, and documents specifically the Romaniote and Sephardic communities. And in the Kaisarianí neighborhood, where in May 1944 two hundred Communist hostages were shot in reprisal, there is a monument at the former shooting range.

closing: Ask, if the occasion arises, about Zakynthos and Bishop Chrysostomos: it is a story that on the Ionian islands is known and told with pride, and observing how it is narrated — what is emphasized, to whom credit is attributed, whether or not the question of why Corfu was different comes up — is an exercise in comparative memory you can carry out over a dinner conversation.

sections.heading: A country split three ways
paragraphs: The German invasion began on April 6, 1941, and within three weeks the front had collapsed. Crete fell in May after history's first great airborne operation, in which the civilian population took part in the resistance with whatever came to hand and suffered immediate, massive reprisals for it.

What followed was not one occupation but three. Germany retained Athens, Salonica, Crete and the strategic points; Italy administered most of the mainland and the Ionian islands — that is, CORFU AND PAXOS WERE ITALIAN between 1941 and September 1943 — and Bulgaria effectively annexed eastern Macedonia and Thrace, with a policy of violent Bulgarianization. The country was carved up, with three administrations, three occupation currencies and three distinct policies toward the population.

That fragmentation matters for understanding what follows: there was no single Greek experience of the occupation but several, and the regional differences of those four years explain much of the subsequent alignments in the civil war. Corfu, under Italian administration until 1943, endured a comparatively less lethal occupation; from September 1943, when Italy capitulated and the Germans took over after bombing the island and disarming the Italian garrison, everything changed.

sections.heading: The famine of 1941–1942: administered scarcity
paragraphs: The winter of 1941–1942 produced in Athens a famine whose mortality estimates range between one hundred thousand and three hundred thousand people across the country as a whole. There are photographs of carts collecting corpses from the streets each morning. It is one of the most severe episodes of urban hunger in twentieth-century Europe, and it is also, analytically, a textbook case.

Greece imported a substantial share of its wheat before the war. The occupation cut off imports, requisitioned production to feed the troops, dismantled internal transport between regions — each occupation zone operated separately — and triggered a hyperinflation that destroyed the value of wages and savings. At the same time, the Allied naval blockade kept food from entering, on the argument that supplying an occupied territory would benefit the enemy. The result was not an absolute shortage of food: there was food in the countryside, there was a black market for whoever could pay, there was rapid enrichment among middlemen. What there was, was a COLLAPSE OF ACCESS for the urban population without income or land.

It is exactly what Amartya Sen formulated in studying famines: they are caused less by the absence of food than by the collapse of entitlements to it. The Greek famine is an especially clear-cut case because it had an identifiable political cause at every link: requisitioning, administrative fragmentation, occupation inflation and Allied blockade. Only from 1942, after an international campaign, did the Swedish and Swiss Red Cross manage to establish a humanitarian corridor with Canadian flour.

The lesson transfers without difficulty. When Peru debates food insecurity in the ollas comunes or hunger in conflict zones, the useful question is not how much food exists in the country but who can gain access to it, and what chain of administrative decisions produces the exclusion.

sections.heading: The mountain: a parallel state with women's suffrage
paragraphs: The Greek resistance was one of the most massive in occupied Europe. EAM, the National Liberation Front, led by the Communist Party but far broader than it, came to encompass a very considerable share of the adult population — the usual estimates speak of more than a million people out of seven and a half million inhabitants — with its armed wing, ELAS. Republican and anti-Communist organizations also existed, chief among them Napoleon Zervas's EDES, strong precisely in Epirus, opposite Corfu.

In the liberated mountain zones, what came to be called Free Greece was organized: people's courts substituting for an absent judicial system, schools, field hospitals, cooperatives, food distribution. In March 1944 PEEA, a mountain government, was formed, and to elect its National Council, elections were held in which WOMEN VOTED.

Pause on that fact. Greek women won the right to vote in national elections in 1952. In the occupied mountains, eight years earlier, they voted, and some were elected. And in the resistance they took part massively as combatants, liaisons, nurses and organizers, in a rupture of the gender order that rural Greek society had never known. After the liberation, that experience was suppressed along with the organization that had made it possible, and the women who had taken part were doubly marked: as leftists, and for having stepped outside their place.

The Peruvian parallel is uncomfortable and true: spaces of war and crisis produce real openings in the gender order — the women of the glass-of-milk committees and the communal kitchens, the leaders of displaced communities, the presidents of mothers' clubs like María Elena Moyano — and those openings are usually later reabsorbed or punished. Emancipation produced by catastrophe rarely survives normalization.

sections.heading: Reprisals and extermination: Kalavryta, Salonica, Corfu
paragraphs: The German doctrine of collective reprisal was applied in Greece with extreme intensity. At Kommeno, in August 1943, more than three hundred inhabitants were killed. At Kalavryta, on December 13, 1943, around seven hundred men and boys of the town were executed and the town itself was burned. At Distomo, in June 1944, more than two hundred people, including children. These are only the best-known of dozens of such cases.

And there is the extermination of the Jewish communities, which in Greece was nearly total. That of Salonica was one of the oldest and largest in Europe: Sephardim who had arrived after the expulsion from Spain in 1492, with their Judeo-Spanish language, their presses, their trade unions, and for centuries the city's single largest group. Between March and August 1943 around forty-six thousand Salonican Jews were deported to Auschwitz; about four percent survived. Earlier, in December 1942, the Jewish cemetery — with hundreds of thousands of graves, one of the oldest in Europe — was destroyed and its stone reused in the city's buildings. The main campus of Aristotle University is built on that ground.

And there is Corfu, which concerns you directly. The Corfiot Jewish community, of mixed Romaniote and Venetian origin, lived in the quarter known as Evraikí, next to the New Fortress. On June 9, 1944 — when the war had already been decided militarily, and three days after the Normandy landings — the German authorities summoned the community, concentrated it in the Old Fortress, shipped it to the mainland and from there to Auschwitz. Of around one thousand nine hundred people, barely more than a hundred survived. The Scuola Greca synagogue survived and still stands, on Velissariou Street, and remains active.

The contrast lies on the neighboring island. In Zakynthos, Mayor Loukas Karrer and Bishop Chrysostomos, faced with the order to hand over the list of the island's Jews, submitted a sheet with two names: their own. The entire community, some two hundred seventy-five people, was hidden in inland villages and survived intact. Two Ionian islands, a short distance apart, two opposite outcomes.

The comparison of these two cases is one of the most precise moral lessons the history of the Holocaust offers, and it should be stated carefully so as not to turn it uplifting. It does not prove that willing it was enough: the conditions were different — the size of the communities, the geography, the moment, the German presence. It proves something more limited and more demanding: that margin existed, that some officials used it and others did not, and that the machinery of extermination needed, in each locality, someone to hand over the list. The bureaucracy of genocide is always local at its last link.

sections.heading: Peruvian mirror: who counts the dead
paragraphs: Peru's internal armed conflict between 1980 and 2000 left, according to the estimate of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission published in 2003, some sixty-nine thousand dead and disappeared, of whom approximately three-quarters had Quechua or another indigenous language as their mother tongue. That figure was itself an event: it was far higher than anyone had reckoned, and it revealed that the country had ignored the magnitude of its own war because the victims were overwhelmingly rural, poor and indigenous.

The structure of the episodes is similar down to the details: Lucanamarca in 1983, Accomarca in 1985, Cayara in 1988, the logic of collective reprisal against an entire village for actions attributed to a few, and the subsequent dispute over the numbers, the names and the legal classification of the events. And the problem of the last link is similar too: in Greece there were Security Battalions, Greek anti-Communist militias armed by the occupier; in Peru there were self-defense committees and local collaborations of varying sorts. Mass violence always needs local participation, and that participation is what national memories are slowest to admit.

There is, however, a decisive difference, and it is worth naming: Greece processed its occupation within a national narrative of resistance that, though selective and disputed, granted its victims the status of martyrs of the nation. Peru never achieved that. Its dead remain, for a considerable part of the country, suspects, and that is precisely the function of terruqueo: to retroactively deny the status of victim. Judith Butler called this the unequal distribution of grief, the question of which lives are grievable. Greece mourned Kalavryta. Peru has not finished mourning Accomarca.
